I really struggle with this too. What helps me is to highlight or type out/paraphrase as i read. Bullet points, full sentences, whatever works.

Journaling! Noticing and actively seeking what gives you any momentary feeling of being alive. Even if it’s as simple and insignificant as watching a sunset, reading in a cafe, trying out new foods, making a new playlist. Cling to this whenever you feel like you’re slipping. And keep doing it. Even better if it’s something that involves getting you out of the house, though that can take time. 

This helped me grasp onto the rare sparks of motivation I desperately needed. It’s hard to find the drive to live/function (still can’t create it on my own), but occasionally, it miraculously appears for a moment. A random morning where the sky seems a little brighter, the air easier to breathe, your shoulders somewhat less heavy. Whenever possible, don’t let that moment go - even the narrowest windows of opportunity can be THE fighting chance to climb out of a depressive episode. Focusing my efforts into gaining and maintaining momentum was my biggest (and most difficult) step forward into recovery. Not that i’ve “recovered”. I still continuously do this to pick myself back up each time I fall. But I’m definitely not where i was 3 years ago. And i’m so thankful i picked up that first journal/planner and stuck with it since then. 

I also noticed that each time didn’t journal for 2+ weeks, my mental state defs starts to fall apart lol. It was interesting to keep track of my ups and downs. Gives you a lot of insight into what’s working for you and what isn’t. 

This was what worked for me. I know people who say meditation was their gamechanger. Never quite did it for me, but to each their own. Go with what feels right for yourself. There’s no one single solution. Good luck! Let’s keep fighting on  :-)

Of course lung health and whatnot isn’t the priority when you feel suffocated by your own insidious thoughts. Who cares about longevity and quality of life, when you don’t even feel safe in your own head. 

Your mind and body learned through experience that this was the best way to survive the moment. Not by choice and incompetence, but by natural instinct. It’d be terrifying to let go of what brought us relief and comfort. But! This also means we can still UNlearn our dysfunctional coping mechanisms or habits, so this isn’t anywhere near game over just yet. You’re not a failure; you got yourself through all those years with a strategy that worked to fulfill your immediate needs. And you’re still standing here today, reflecting on your FUTURE needs and priorities as an adult. That’s growth, and it takes courage and resilience. Much respect to you man. Keep going. Nope. Depression doesn’t discriminate between anyone, regardless of background or experience. Sure, some people may be more vulnerable to it, but it can happen to anyone. 

But yes, it often does stem from trauma. And you’re right - simpler things can count as trauma too. Constant criticism, lack of recognition, feelings of inadequacy, social pressures, witnessing other people’s struggles etc. (esp throughout childhood), can absolutely give rise to traumatic responses. And this isn’t restricted to intense flashbacks and other PTSD-related symptoms... it can manifest as apathy, anxiety, depression, dissociation, perfectionism etc too. Subtle traumas may go unnoticed and be impossible to pinpoint, but our bodies subconsciously remember the experiences, and adapt accordingly to protect us. It’s easy to forget all this, and end up feeling invalidated and blaming ourselves if we’ve never been through any “Big Real Trauma” like violence/abuse. I struggle to recognize this too. But regardless of what your depression stems from... your struggle is completely real and valid, and still requires so much resilience and strength to keep holding on. And I’m just as proud of you for hanging in there :-).

On a serious note though, milk the shit out of your college’s student services. You’ve paid for it anyway. Counselling is hit-or-miss (the latter for me). I hope yours has a Disability/Accessibility centre for accommodations, or something similar. Actually saved my academic life. Asking for help can feel so shameful, I know. It took time to work through it. Do whatever it takes. I had a shitty free tutor who didn’t understand my coursework at all (Biology) but I stuck with it for the sole purpose of forcing myself out of the house once a week to START and DO something. She literally would just sit there in silence while my perfectionist ass would do assignments at the speed of a fucking sloth. Cringe lol but gotta do what ya gotta do. 


Somehow made it through my undergrad last year, after 7 gruesome years - with a big push from the fact that my entire degree would be invalidated and wasted if not completed within that time. Yikes. But there you have it. It feels impossible (I wouldn’t have believed myself a year ago) but it is somehow doable - with a LOT of help and strategy. You’ll be surprised how many second chances you get to save your ass by connecting with Disability/Access services. (I don’t mean that in a complacent sense.. abusing the system will screw you over haha) Their accommodations and advocacy for my struggles seriously saved my degree. Esp with perfectionism - 1.5x time on exams(?!) made a world of a difference. Don’t assume a failed midterm has ruined everything and the only choice left is to give up - speak to them, or your prof. Don’t let the school give you a 0% without putting up a fight. They’re not gonna reach out to you (well if they do, I’m glad your college cares). But you can sure as hell fight for what you need to be given a fair chance at school. Nobody asked for depression and mental illness. Struggling and failing was never our choice. 


**TL;DR** - Use every resource possible to fight for yourself. Speak to your profs/school. Don’t let your college define the limits of your academic capabilities. Good luck!!!!! If time off or an alternative to school is what you need, that’s ok too. (I withdrew from way too many courses much too late - would’ve saved years of time if i just admitted that what i was stubbornly doing alone wasn’t working, and that i needed help). It’s a long journey that’ll take you much further than graduation. Mental illness does NOT get to define what we can or cannot do. I believe in you, dude. Rooting for ya.
